title: Task Alignment Outweighs Framework Choice in Scientific LLM Agents
experiments_summary: The study employed the Corral framework, a modular benchmarking system implementing a Language Decision Process (POMDP-based) architecture, to systematically evaluate LLM-based agents across four expert-designed scientific environments: Spectra (molecular structure elucidation from spectroscopic data), Molecular Dynamics (LAMMPS-based simulations), OpenCatalyst (catalyst slab-adsorbate configuration), and Machine Learning (XGBoost model for materials property prediction). Two agent scaffolds were compared: ReAct (thought-action-observation loop) and tool-calling (direct function execution). Two foundation models were tested: Claude-3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o. Tasks were evaluated in two formats: single tasks (K) and chained/decomposed tasks (task groups G), where complex problems were broken into sequential sub-tasks with dependencies. Performance was measured using pass@5 and pass∧5 metrics with binary rewards. Ablation studies were conducted on tool description verbosity at three levels (BRIEF, WORKFLOW, COMPREHENSIVE) by programmatically filtering structured docstring tags. To investigate tool-task alignment, tool and task descriptions were embedded and pairwise distances were computed to correlate with agent performance across environments. A hypothesis-generator tool was added to the Spectra environment to test whether closing the tool-task embedding distance improved performance. Additional metrics tracked included token usage (prompt, completion, total), tool call success/failure rates (classified as invalid_tool, invalid_args, or execution_error), and execution time. Tasks were manually classified by domain experts into five categories: retrieval, code execution, experiment execution, reasoning, and validation, and average pass@5 scores were computed per category across chained tasks.
